newsitem.title: INDIA: Erratic rains hit oilseeds, rice sowing in India.
newsitem.headline: Erratic rains hit oilseeds, rice sowing in India.

text.p: Indian sowing operations have been hit due to deficient monsoon rain in the oilseeds growing areas and excess rain in some rice belts, experts and trade officials said on Wednesday.

"Monsoon has not really set in in some oilseeds growing areas," S.M. Virmani, an agriculture expert at the Hyderabad-based International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics, told Reuters.
Virmani said sowing operations had been affected in the central regions due to deficient rains. "Sowing in the central plateau is very, very small."
Central Madhya Pradesh state accounts for about 80 percent of the country's soybean output.
Virmani said initial monsoon rains were just enough to cultivate the seed-bed. Thereafter, rainfall had not been adequate, he said.

A.V.R. Krishna Rao, a senior official at the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) told Reuters that rainfall was adequate in most parts of the country except in some regions in central India, parts of southern states and in the northern state of Jammu and Kashmir.
"We hope that the deficiency will be wiped out to a large extent during this week," Rao said.
Navinbhai Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange said oilseeds sowing had been hit in the southern states of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu due to deficient monsoon rains.
"Sowing is not very promising in these areas," Shah said. The three southern states account for nearly 50 percent of the country's groundnut production.

Shah said Saurashtra region in western Gujarat state had received good initial monsoon rains, which helped sowing operations, but thereafter rainfall was deficient affecting seed germination. "The newly sown seeds are moisture-starved," Shah said.
The Saurashtra region in Gujarat state accounts for 35 percent of the country's groundnut output.

"If we do not get plentiful rains in the next 10 days in all oilseed growing areas, then there will be drastic changes in the Kharif (winter) crop estimates," he said. India annually harvests two oilseeds crops.
Trade officials have estimated the winter oilseeds crop for 1997/98 at 12.5 million tonnes.
Virmani said excess rain in the eastern state of Bihar and some northeastern states had caused floods in the rice growing fields that had delayed sowing operations.

"Except Orissa, sowing had been delayed in other eastern and northeasten states," Virmani said. In India, 30 percent of the rice cultivation is on rain-fed lands and the remainder is on irrigated lands.
Rao said 26 out of 35 sub-divisions in the country had received excess or normal rainfall. IMD has divided the country into 35 sub-divisions based on a specific rainfall pattern.
Rao said that the EL Nino warm water currents, which was threatening crops across Asia, was unlikely to affect India's monsoon rains further.
"We stand by our original forecast on El Nino," Rao said.

IMD, when giving its monsoon forecast in May had predicted that monsoon rains in India would be slightly on the negative side of the long-term average as El Nino was showing an "unfavourable trend" this year.
